procedures.impact_note: A file that is too permissive can expose secrets in it to local users; one with the wrong owner or group can stop the IPA service that needs it from reading it.
procedures.limitations: This sets only the owner, group or mode ipa-healthcheck reports; it does not change SELinux labels. If a service still cannot read the file afterwards, check 'ls -Z' and 'ausearch -m avc'. When ipa-healthcheck accepts more than one value, the change would add permissions, or the owner is not an IPA service account, no fix is chosen for you. The checks describe the file as it was when ipa-diagnose ran: run the commands straight away, and run ipa-diagnose again if anything may have changed since (chown -h and chgrp -h do not follow a link at the file itself, but directories on the way are followed).

procedures.limitations: This fixes this host's clock only. Kerberos compares two clocks; if another machine's clock is wrong, fix it there. It does not explain why the clock drifted (for example a blocked NTP port).

This host's clock is {ref.tracking.offset_abs} s {ref.tracking.direction} its time source, well inside Kerberos' 300 s tolerance, so it cannot by itself explain a clock-skew error. Compare 'chronyc tracking' on the KDC and on the other machine; the wrong clock is probably there.
chronyd has not synchronized with a time source (leap status {ref.tracking.leap_status}), so the time it would step to is not trustworthy. Fix NTP first.
chronyd reports no reference source, so the time it would step to is not trustworthy.

The measured offset is more than a day ({ref.tracking.offset_abs} s). Stepping an IPA server's clock that far can make certificates look expired; confirm the time source is right before changing anything.
